## Interest

In finance you never do anything for free and you would always prefer 
to have money now rather than later.  For example, if you are loaning 
someone money, you would expect to be compensated for the fact that you are giving up the opportunity to use that money for some other purpose.  This is the **time value of money** and the compensation is called **interest**.

:::{.definition data-title="Interest"}
**Interest** is the cost of borrowing money or the return on investment for
lending money.  It is typically expressed as a percentage of the principal
amount over a specified period of time.
:::

Suppose we loan initial amount (the **principal**) $P$ to a borrower to hold 
for some period of time.  To compensate us for the use of our money, the 
borrower agrees to pay us interest at an agreed rate $r$.  Their interest 
**accrues** when the amount of interest earned on an investment is added 
to the principal.  The total amount owed at the end of the loan period is 
called the **future value** $F$ of the loan.  

How much interest is earned depends on the rate, number of repayments $m$
(more typically determined from loan duration $T$ and repayment frequency 
$T/n$), and whether the interest is **simple** or **compound**. 

### Simple vs Compound Interest

In **simple interest**, the interest is calculated only on the principal amount

$$
F_s = P(1 + rm).
$$

:::{.definition data-title="Compound Interest"}

In compound interest, the interest is calculated on the accrued total 
(principal + interest)

$$
F_c = P(1 + r)^m.
$$

:::

:::{.example data-title="Interest Rates"}
Suppose we loan $P=\$100$ at a monthly interest rate of $r=1.5\%$ for $n=12$ 
months.  The future value of the loan under simple and compound interest is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_s & = 100(1 + 0.015 \cdot 12) = 100(1 + 0.18) = 100(1.18) = \$118 \\
F_c & = 100(1 + 0.015)^{12} \approx 100(1.195618) \approx \$119.56.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

### Annualization

In finance, interest rates are often expressed on an annual basis, even if the
interest is compounded more frequently. 

:::{.definition data-title="Nominal Interest Rate"}

The nominal rate $r^{(m)}$ is a stated annual rate that is *compounded $m$ 
times per year*. It is quoted as a yearly figure, but interest is actually
credited every $1/m$ of a year at the periodic rate

$$
\text{periodic rate} = \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}.
$$

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Effective Interest Rate"}

The effective annual rate $r$ is the single once-a-year rate that produces 
the same growth as the nominal rate over one year. Since $1$ dollar grows to
$\left(1+\frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m$ after one year with $m$ compounding 
periods,

$$
1 + r = \left(1 + \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r = \left(1 + \frac{r^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m - 1.
$$

:::

In North American consumer finance, the effective annual rate is called APY (annual percentage yield) for savings. The nominal rate on loans is called APR (annual percentage rate), which is usually just the periodic rate times the number of periods, so it understates the true cost relative to the effective rate.  The process of converting a nomial rate to an effective annual 
rate is called **annualization**.  The main purpose of annualization is to provide a standardized way to compare interest rates across different financial products and investment opportunities.  It allows investors and borrowers to make informed decisions by understanding the true cost or return of a financial product over a one-year period.

:::{.example data-title="Annualization"}

Suppose we take out a loan with a nominal interest rate of $r^{(12)} = 6\%$
compounded monthly.  The effective annual rate is given by

$$
r = \left(1 + \frac{0.06}{12}\right)^{ 12} - 1 \approx 0.061678 - 1 \approx 0.061678 \approx 6.17\%.
$$

:::

### Continuous Compounding

Continuous compounding is the limit of the nominal-rate setup as the number 
of compounding periods per year $m \to \infty$. Interest is effectively 
credited over infinitesimally small periods, and the effective annual rate
approaches an upper limit of $e^r - 1$.

Start with $A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^{mt}$ and take logs:

$$
\ln\frac{A}{P} = mt\,\ln\!\left(1+\frac{r}{m}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\,m\to\infty\,}\; rt,
$$

since $\ln(1+x) \sim x$ as $x \to 0$. Exponentiating gives

$$
A = P\,e^{rt}.
$$

One can reach the same result by applying L’Hôpital’s rule to the logarithm 
of the growth factor. There is no $m$ in the formula: a common error is to 
carry $n$ into the continuous formula, but $e^{rt}$ already accounts for
infinitely frequent compounding.

In actuarial notation, the continuously compounded rate is called the 
**force of interest** $\delta$. The accumulation function is 
$a(t) = e^{\int_0^t \delta(s)\,ds}$, which reduces to $e^{\delta t}$ when
$\delta$ is constant. Equivalently, $\delta$ is the logarithmic derivative 
of the accumulation function: 

$$
\delta(t) = \frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}.
$$

With a constant force of interest,

$$
1 + i = e^{\delta}, \qquad \delta = \ln(1+i), \qquad \delta = \lim_{m\to\infty} i^{(m)}.$$

The force of interest is below the effective annual rate but above the 
effective discount rate. In terms of the nominal rates from before, 
$i^{(m)}$ decreases toward $\delta$ as $m$ grows:

$$i > i^{(2)} > i^{(4)} > i^{(12)} > \cdots > \delta.$$

Converting a continuous rate to an effective annual rate (APY) is just 
$e^{r}-1$. At $r = 6\%$ this gives about $6.184\%$. Using the 12% nominal
example from earlier: calcfyi

| Compounding	| Effective annual rate |
| - | - |
| Annual ($m=1$) |	$12.000\%$ |
| Monthly ($m=12$)	| $12.683\%$ |
| Continuous ($m\to\infty$) |	$e^{0.12}-1 \approx 12.750\%$ |


Most of the gain from more frequent compounding comes by $m=12$. Daily and continuous compounding differ by under a dollar in one worked example, so continuous compounding is used mainly for mathematical convenience. calcfyi

:::{.example data-title="Continuous Compounding"}

Investing $1000 at 8% for 5 years gives $1000\,e^{0.4} \approx \$1491.82$ under continuous compounding, versus $1469.33 with annual compounding. calcfyi

To find a doubling time, solve $e^{\delta t} = 2$:

$$t = \frac{\ln 2}{\delta}.$$

:::
